summary: IB Design Technology extended response: decode command terms, make a two-minute plan, structure analysis, evaluate evidence, and capture every available mark.
body_markdown:
An **IB Design Technology extended response** tests whether you can select relevant design knowledge, apply it to a context, develop an argument, and reach a supported judgement under time pressure.


A page of accurate theory can still miss the task if it never addresses the named product, user, material, or manufacturing process. Strong answers make those connections explicit.


The method is straightforward: decode the question, make a brief plan, develop distinct points, and check that your response satisfies the command term.


### The extended-response checklist


Before writing:


- Identify the **command term** , content, and design context.
- Use the available marks to judge the required depth.
- Spend up to two minutes planning distinct points.
- Apply technical knowledge to the named situation.
- Include trade-offs or alternatives where required.
- Finish with a supported judgement when appropriate.


RevisionDojo's guide to[common Design Technology command terms](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-command-terms-appear-most-in-ib-design-technology-exams) helps clarify the differences between *explain* , *analyse* , and *evaluate* .


### Decode the question before recalling content


Under pressure, it is tempting to recognize a topic and immediately write everything you remember. But the topic identifies the knowledge you need; the command term determines how to use it.


Separate the prompt into three parts: **command** , **content** , and **context** . The context might specify a user group, production scale, environment, or design objective.


Suppose you must evaluate injection moulding for a reusable chair produced at high volume. Defining the process establishes knowledge, but evaluation requires weighing its suitability. High tooling costs may be justified by production volume, while repeatability supports consistent dimensions. Material choice, repairability, design changes, and recovery arrangements may complicate the decision.


The[RevisionDojo extended-response guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-do-you-answer-extended-response-questions-in-ib-design-technology) reinforces this applied rhythm: make a point, explain its consequence, and connect it to the design context.


### Make a two-minute plan


Planning prevents a costly discovery halfway through writing: every paragraph is making the same point.


A student urges their ambitious brain to finish planning within two minutes


For the chair example, your notes could identify repeatability, complex forms, tooling costs, and environmental considerations. Add a provisional judgement: suitable if demand is stable and material recovery is credible.


This is a decision map. Each note gives a paragraph a distinct purpose. If two notes lead to the same consequence, combine them before writing.


Select points you can develop accurately. Several disconnected claims rarely demonstrate as much understanding as a smaller set of explained, applied arguments. Use RevisionDojo's guide to[managing Design Technology exam time](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-do-you-manage-time-in-ib-design-technology-exams) when allocating planning, writing, and checking time.


### Structure the IB Design Technology extended response


Use this paragraph structure as a flexible guide:


Element What to write


Point A claim addressing the question


Knowledge A relevant principle, property, or process


Application Its significance for the named situation


Consequence The resulting benefit, limitation, or decision


For example:


> Injection moulding can produce repeatable chair components. Consistent dimensions matter in high-volume production because variation could slow assembly or affect stability. However, expensive tooling makes the process less attractive if demand is uncertain or frequent design changes are expected.


Each sentence advances the argument. The technical knowledge earns its place by explaining a design consequence.


### Match your reasoning to the command term


For **explain** , establish how or why something happens. Words such as “because” and “therefore” help reveal causal relationships.


For **analyse** , examine relevant parts and their relationships. Show how material properties, manufacturing constraints, user needs, cost, and performance interact.


For **evaluate** , weigh strengths and limitations, then judge which factors matter most in the context. Adding “however” once does not establish evaluation.


For **justify** , defend a choice using relevant evidence or design criteria. Explain why it suits the stated requirements, considering realistic alternatives where useful.


Clear analytical paragraphs are more useful than an elaborate introduction. The guide to[common Design Technology exam mistakes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-are-the-most-common-ib-design-technology-exam-mistakes) helps identify habits that weaken otherwise accurate answers.


### Turn description into design analysis


Description identifies a property. Analysis explains its significance.


Saying aluminium has relatively low density is descriptive. Connecting that property to reduced product mass, easier handling, and the needs of a particular user develops analysis. Considering cost, durability, forming, or embodied impact introduces relevant trade-offs.


Return to the question's specific requirements. For an outdoor mobility product for older users, consider exposure, safety, comfort, maintenance, and handling. These anchors keep your reasoning relevant.


Use[IB Design Technology Study Notes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-design-technology) to strengthen technical knowledge. Flashcards support recall, while AI Chat can prompt you to explain why a fact changes a design decision.


### Check with a marker's questions


Reserve a final minute to check:


- Have I fulfilled the command term?
- Does each major point address the context?
- Have I explained consequences rather than listed features?
- Does my judgement follow from my argument?
- Have I repeated a point without developing it?


There is no universal sentence-per-mark formula. Follow your current syllabus materials, specimen questions, and teacher guidance. Assessment documentation differs between the older course and the course first assessed in 2027, so confirm which applies to you.


### Practise until the method becomes familiar


Begin with an untimed answer. Annotate your knowledge, application, analysis, and judgement. Then attempt another response under a time limit, focusing on the weakest element.


RevisionDojo brings this cycle together through its Questionbank, Study Notes, and feedback tools. Use Grading tools to review development, Tutors to investigate recurring difficulties, and Predicted Papers or Mock Exams for timed practice. The Coursework Library can provide examples of communicated design reasoning, while exam answers must remain focused on the prompt.


Start with the[Design Technology Questionbank](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-design-technology-new) , then use[Design Technology Paper 2 revision guidance](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-should-you-revise-for-ib-design-technology-paper-2) to extend the method into timed sessions. The aim is to make deliberate reasoning available even when the clock feels demanding.
